newsitem.title: USA: FASB chief unruffled by derivatives flap.
newsitem.headline: FASB chief unruffled by derivatives flap.

text.p: For Financial Accounting Standards Board Chairman Dennis Beresford, dealing with torrents of criticism is all in a day's work.

That's fortunate, because these days Beresford's work involves sorting through sharply critical feedback as the FASB fine-tunes its controversial attempt to impose uniform accounting standards on the use of derivatives and hedging by U.S. companies.
Accounting standards are important because derivatives have become very big business for corporations and financial institutions.

The face amount, or notional value, of derivatives grew by $782 billion during the third quarter of 1996 to $19.8 trillion -- of which $8.3 trillion was in futures and forwards, $7.3 trillion in swaps and $4.2 trillion in options, according to the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of Currency.

Since the FASB issued its proposed overhaul in June many corporate finance chiefs and futures exchange officials have voiced fears that the changes would lead to more volatile earnings and jittery investors.
The complaints poured in -- in some 275 letters and also during four days of public hearings in November at which representatives of 40 companies and organisations spoke.
"I guess we were hoping, after all the time and effort we put into this document, that it might have been received somewhat better than it has been," Beresford admitted.
The seven-member accounting board will take all the criticisms into account when it begins three months of intensive deliberations starting Wednesday, Beresford said in an interview.
A final document is expected by June 30, he said.
Derivatives are the complicated financial instruments that have figured in several well-publicised scandals and investments-turned-sour in recent years.
The FASB is seeking to require companies to carry all derivatives on their balance sheets at current market value.

Under current practice, many derivatives -- instruments whose value is based on the value of another instrument, asset or market index -- are carried off-balance sheet, and similar transactions may receive disparate accounting treatment.
Most of the criticism stems from the accounting board's proposed treatment of changes in the value of derivatives once they are carried on balance sheets.

"The area where we will spend the greatest amount of time -- and the greatest chance for change in the (June) exposure draft -- is on whether the gain or loss associated with recognising a derivative at fair value would be recognised in the income statement," said Beresford.
He said there is general agreement in the financial community that improved accounting guidance is needed for derivatives and hedging.
"And a reasonable number of people have agreed with (FASB's proposal of) printing them in the balance sheet at fair value," he said.
The disagreements occur in the details, he said.
"If you came to one of our regular board meetings, you'd find there is just as much disagreement (within FASB) on some of these issues as there is between us and the constituents."
The accounting board has no government authority, but is a private organisation whose pronouncements on accounting are recognised as authoritative by the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Beresford said changes in accounting standards are inherently controversial and bound to upset some people.
"If we had some sort of a (meter) that measured the degree of controversy, this (derivatives debate) would be certainly above the mid-point."
